Noteworthy of tropical climates throughout the world is the uniformity of temperature and length of daylight throughout the year. Rainfall varies from a distinct seasonal distribution in some regions to constant and very heavy in others. The flora and fauna of the tropical forest is marked by the richness of their species composition. Correlated with this is the harshness and severity of interspecific competition and predation. With uniform climate throughout the year, cold-blooded animals may have several generations per year and species of birds, though not the same individuals, may breed during every month. There is no hibernation or period of dormancy, nor is there migration. Cold-blooded forms, especially reptiles, reach a large size in the tropics, but birds and mammals are generally smaller than their relatives in temperate regions.
Species with widespread distribution: About 20 percent of the species and subspecies appearing in the 1973 U.S. "Red Book" are wide ranging in distribution being characteristic of one biome or ranging over two or more biomes. (Appendix E). Relationships with a biome are based upon the historical distribution of the species rather than its present endangered distribution. Most of the birds in this group are migratory. Following are brief descriptions of the distribution of selected species of this group showing how their restoration may affect the U.S. environment.
The <u>California condor</u>, although now confined to a small range in southern California, once was distributed from the Columbia River on the Oregon-Washington border, south to northern Baja, California and east to southwest Utah and Arizona.
